claims.text: Stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations in tungsten refractory high-entropy-alloy intermediate layers will enhance heat-transfer capability while maintaining structural integrity.
CrFeTiTa-based and VFeTiTaW refractory high-entropy alloys can be produced by mechanical alloying and sintering for use as reactor interlayers.
The proposed starting materials have baseline thermal conductivity and mechanical properties typical of as-sintered samples.
A controlled heat treatment can trigger SCCPs in the proposed intermediate-layer alloys.
The nanoprecipitate composition can be optimized to maximize thermal conduction.
The proposed improvement should persist at operating temperatures up to 800 °C.
The proposed improvement should persist under steady-state heat fluxes around 10 MW/m², transient fluxes up to 20 MW/m², and cyclic thermal stress.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as microscale thermal bridges within the matrix.
The nanoprecipitates increase local thermal conductivity through improved electron/phonon coupling.
Coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and reduce stress concentrations that could initiate premature cracking.
SCCP-treated layers will exhibit more than a 10% increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to the as-sintered baseline.
SCCP-treated layers will maintain or improve tensile strength and ductility relative to the as-sintered baseline.
Intermediate layers without nanoprecipitate enhancement have lower thermal conductivity and greater susceptibility to thermal-stress buildup.
The proposed outcome is limited to tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys whose compositions support stable coherent nanoprecipitates.
The optimal nanoprecipitate phases and spatial distributions have not yet been established.
Nanoprecipitate-mediated thermal-conductivity gains may need to be balanced against potential embrittlement.
A controlled comparison should use heat-treated SCCP samples and otherwise comparable as-sintered samples subjected to cyclic and transient high-heat-flux testing.
The hypothesis is falsified if treated samples fail to achieve a statistically significant thermal-conductivity improvement of at least 10% without loss of mechanical integrity relative to controls.
